habitat: James's Flamingos inhabit extremely high-altitude Andean salt lakes above 3,500 meters in Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina — the highest-altitude flamingo habitat on Earth in South America. They frequent shallow, saline or alkaline lakes, coastal lagoons, mudflats, and estuaries. Like all flamingos, they require extensive shallow water bodies with abundant microscopic algae and invertebrates for feeding, as well as isolated islands, mud bars, and salt flats for nesting. Their habitat is characterized by extreme conditions — high salinity and alkalinity that most other bird species cannot tolerate — which provides protection from terrestrial predators and reduces competition for food.
diet: James's Flamingos are filter feeders, consuming algae (particularly Spirulina and diatoms), small crustaceans (brine shrimp, copepods), mollusks, and aquatic insect larvae. Their pink coloration comes from carotenoid pigments in their diet, primarily beta-carotene from algae and canthaxanthin from crustaceans. They feed upside-down, submerging their head and sweeping it through the water while filtering food particles with their specialized beak. They may consume up to 20-30% of their body weight daily in wet food.
behavior: James's Flamingos are highly social, living and nesting in enormous colonies ranging from hundreds to tens of thousands of birds. Their synchronous courtship displays — involving head-flagging, wing-salutes, twist-preening, and mass marching — are among nature's most spectacular avian performances. Pairs are seasonally monogamous, jointly constructing conical mud nests and incubating a single egg. Both parents produce 'crop milk' — a red, nutritious secretion — to feed the chick. Flamingos are strong fliers, traveling up to 500 km in a single night between feeding and breeding sites.
facts: James's Flamingos can stand on one leg for hours without muscle fatigue — their leg joints have a locking mechanism that reduces energy expenditure. Their pink coloration intensifies with diet; captive flamingos may fade to pale pink or white without carotenoid supplementation. They can live 25-40 years in the wild and over 50 in captivity. Their distinctive downward-curved beak contains lamellae (comb-like structures) that filter microscopic food particles from the water. Flamingo chicks are born gray or white and take 2-3 years to achieve full pink plumage.
naming: Flamingo names might reflect their striking pink color, elegant stance, or colony lifestyle. Consider names like Coral, Flamingo, Pinky, Rose, Sunset, Laguna, Flamenco, Salsa, Hibiscus, Sorbet, or Tango.
